A pod taller than the fae split along one seam, its two halves curled right back like a boat hull, packed white silk standing in a solid block, already lifting off the top in a slow column, the inner face pearl-smooth and catching light.

A fat green pod swollen drum-tight, its seams lifting along both sides under real pressure, ready to spring at a touch — and beside it the same pod after, its shell coiled into a stiff papery spiral, one seed still caught in the coil.

A dandelion head as wide across as the fae is tall, a hundred tufts packed so close the globe is solid, each seed on its own thin stalk under a crown of fine white down, lit from behind into one sphere of white fire.

A head down to a pale pitted ring of sockets, woody and regular as a honeycomb section, with one last tuft still caught in it at a crooked angle, the rim of the ring bright where the light catches it.

A dry ribbed head the colour of old bone, three slits opened along its top, tipped over by two hands so seeds pour out of the slits in a fast rattling stream, the grooved walls vibrating with each shake.

A seed-ball bristling all over with fine hooks, each hook curled at its tip, as big across as the fae's head, every hook already gripping a scrap of something — a fleck of lichen, a moth-wing scale, a single amber leaf-hair.

A bunch of paired papery blade-seeds hanging in pairs from one stem, each blade as long as the fae's arm, papery tan, veins standing dark through it where light comes through, the fat bead of a nut at every base, the whole bunch clattering.

A pod split wide, its two halves curling back like stiff wings, the white silk inside lit through to a warm rose-gold where it thins at the edges, a solid column of it still lifting off the top faster than two hands can close on it.

A head down to a woody knob with three last tufts still stuck fast to one side, the knob itself ribbed and amber-pale, each remaining tuft lit from behind into a ring of white fire at its crown, the stem below it hard and green.

A fat pod gone off, its shell now coiled into a tight papery spiral the colour of old straw, one half still attached at the tip, the whole thing torqued hard and vibrating, a single seed visible wedged in the innermost coil.

A dandelion head down to sixty tufts on the windward side, the remaining ones all streaming one direction, each crown of fine white down lit into a separate flare, the socket ring showing pale and pitted in the gaps between them.

A paired papery blade-seed as long as the fae's arm, its papery blade held flat between two hands, veins fanning dark through the wing where light comes through it, the fat round nut at its base still warm amber, the wing glowing rose-gold at its thin edge.

A seed-ball as big as the fae's head, every hook on its surface gripping a catch of fine fibre, a grass-cord strand wrapped twice around it where someone has tried to net it, the cord already sliding off one side.

A pod taller than the fae, its seam split from base to tip, both halves curled right back, the inner face of each half smooth and cream-white, the white silk inside it thinner at the top where the first column has already lifted and gone.

A dry poppy head, hard and blue-grey, its crown of slits wide open, held upside down over a folded-bark scoop, seeds pouring through the slits in a fast bronze stream, the scoop already trembling with the weight of them.

A globe of tufts a hundred thick, two hands pressing in on the near side so twenty tufts spring free at once, each one as big across as the fae's head, the whole near face of the globe lit through to white fire at the moment of release.

A bunch of papery blade-seeds in pairs, each blade as long as the fae's arm, clattering against each other in a steady shove of air, every blade lit warm tan with its veins a dark fan through it, the nuts at their bases knocking together like small bells.

A pod split along one seam, its halves curling back like a stiff boat hull, the silk inside it standing upright and lit through from behind into a column of warm white, one lock of it already unwinding off the top in a fast upward stream.

A seed-ball as big as the fae's head, bristling all over with fine curled hooks, snagged fast by six of them to a rough patch of bark, pulled sideways and held there, every hook on the snagged side bent hard against the grain of the bark.

A head down to a ring of pale sockets, each socket a neat round pit in the woody face, the ring itself the colour of old bone and rimmed with light, a single tuft still lodged in one socket at an angle, its crown of down lit to a white flare.

A fat unopened pod, its seams raised in two pale ridges along its sides, drum-tight and trembling, one hand laid flat against it feeling the pressure underneath, the skin of the pod taut and green and faintly glossy along the ridge where it is closest to splitting.

A dry ribbed head tipped on its side, hard and ochre-brown, its slits rattling as seeds run out of them, a folded-leaf pail underneath it with a round river pebble set on the lip to hold the leaf-lid down against the stream.

A dandelion head as wide across as the fae is tall, its near side pressed in by two hands so the tufts spring out under the palms, a hundred of them packing the globe solid, the whole mass lit from behind into one warm sphere, the pressed side denting like a ripe fruit.

A split pod with its halves curled fully back, the inner face of each half smooth and cream-pale, the silk gone from the top two-thirds, the lowest third still packed tight and lit through from behind into a warm rose-white glow where it thins.

A bunch of paired papery blade-seeds, each blade as long as the fae's arm, four pairs still hanging from the stem and clattering in a steady shove of air, each blade going tan-to-rose at its thin outer edge where light comes through the veins in a dark fan.
